content.intro: This lesson introduces git and software supply-chain integrity as part of Git Security and Professional Best Practices. It follows the supplied Git curriculum and adds an original explanation, an inspectable command example, troubleshooting notes, and a practice task.
content.why_it_matters: Software supply-chain integrity depends on verifiable source, review, controlled credentials, build provenance and artifact verification. Git signatures help with part of this picture but do not prove that code is safe.

content_blocks.title: Signature verification and trust
content_blocks.alt_text: A valid signature proves that the signed payload verifies with a key; trust in who controls that key requires a separate identity and policy check.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Software supply-chain integrity depends on verifiable source, review, controlled credentials, build provenance and artifact verification. Git signatures help with part of this picture but do not prove that code is safe.

For **Git and Software Supply-Chain Integrity**, keep the named subtopics in view: Commit provenance; Signed release tags; Trust boundaries; Verifying the source of project changes. Treat those as the scope of this lesson, then practise the smallest workflow that demonstrates the idea.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: **Before you run a command:** decide what state you are inspecting or changing, identify whether the effect is local or remote, and write down what evidence would count as success. Signatures and object integrity answer different questions. Confirm trusted identity and release provenance independently; an unsigned tag can make verification fail.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Start with git status --short --branch. For destructive or history-rewriting operations, review the exact target, create a recovery reference when appropriate, and keep valuable work backed up. Never put credentials, access tokens or private keys in course submissions.

common_mistakes.problem: Running a state-changing command without confirming the target repository or branch.
common_mistakes.why: A command may affect the wrong working tree or move a reference that other work depends on.
common_mistakes.fix: Check git rev-parse --show-toplevel and git status --short --branch before proceeding.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a command succeeded because no error was visible.
common_mistakes.why: Some Git commands are silent on success, and some expected actions are blocked by repository state or permissions.
common_mistakes.fix: Verify status, log, references, remote state or the named output explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example placeholder literally or applying a destructive example to valuable work.
common_mistakes.why: Paths, branch names and object IDs depend on the current repository; restore/reset/clean operations can discard work.
common_mistakes.fix: Substitute real practice values, use a disposable repository, and preview changes before proceeding.
